title: Challenging the N-Heuristic: read the diagnostic claim with its conditions

source.name: Li, Liu, Gao & Cohen (2024), Challenging the N-Heuristic: Effect size, not sample size, predicts the replicability of psychological science — DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0306911
source.text:
Critically, our goal is not to test whether large N causes greater replicability. Clearly, for a
given study, larger N will increase statistical power and thus the likelihood of identifying a true
effect. Our goal is diagnostic: Is large N a useful diagnostic for assessing the likely replicability
of a research study? In this way, our research is akin to an epidemiological study. An epidemi-
ologist might be interested in a problem, such as suicide, and look for correlates of the problem
(e.g., living in urban vs. rural regions). If living in a rural rather than an urban setting predicted
higher rates of suicide, this would provide useful information regarding where the problem
tends to occur—and where resources and attention should be allocated.

studies were included in our analyses for sample size and 284 in our analysis of effect size (due

We defined effect size in terms of Cohen’s d of the original effect: the mean difference
between the key treatment and control conditions, divided by the standard deviation.

thread.text: Question: Does original sample size work as a diagnostic of which psychological effects replicate? This is a cross-study predictive question, not an intervention increasing N within a fixed study.

Design: pooled replication records supply 307 studies for sample-size analyses and 284 for effect-size analyses. Original effect size is converted to Cohen’s d; the main outcome is binary replication success.

Finding with qualification: separately, N is not a significant predictor and effect size is. When log N and log effect size enter together, both significantly predict replication, consistent with suppression.
A separate survey of 215 scientists rates N above effect size. Neither dataset is representative, and the study does not identify causal effects of editorial policies.

sections.title: Introduction: distinguish diagnosis from causation
sections.role: Frames why a theoretically beneficial N increase need not identify more replicable studies across a varied literature.

points.text: Holding a study’s other attributes fixed is a different comparison from comparing studies that differ in N, effect size and design.

sections.title: Method: define the unit and outcome
sections.role: Connects pooled study records, original-study predictors, exclusions and replication criteria.

points.text: The analysis counts differ: 307 for N, 284 for d. Missing effect-size information prevents treating all models as the same complete sample.
Cohen’s d is the treatment-control mean difference divided by a standard deviation; diverse project measures are reduced to a binary common outcome.

Robustness is not uniform statistical significance: using the Bayesian replication definition available for 54 studies, the effect-size association was rs=.27, p=.057; sample size was rs=-.23, p=.119. The direction is compatible with the main pattern, but the effect-size result does not cross the conventional .05 threshold.

sections.title: Results: the suppressor qualification matters
sections.role: Keeps simple associations, separate adjusted models and a joint model distinct.

points.text: Across effects, the N association is rs = -0.02, p = .741; the d association is rs = .21, p < .001. These are correlations with observed replication success.
Separate design-adjusted logistic models report N B=.20, SE=.16, p=.214 and d B=.64, SE=.23, p=.006; these are not effect sizes on a common standardized scale.

Large N studies investigated smaller effects (rs=-.49, p<.001), found post hoc. In the joint log-predictor model, N B=.56, SE=.20, p=.005 and d B=1.03, SE=.28, p=.0002. Thus the paper does not show N is irrelevant.

sections.learning_goal: Distinguish the separate and joint predictor models, and explain why these diagnostic associations do not show N is causally irrelevant

purpose.text: See what the plotted comparison actually estimates.

reading.text: Original PDF page7: x-axis names sample size and effect size; y-axis is Coefficient Estimate. Points come from separate logistic regressions controlling design; bars are 95% confidence intervals, not ±1 SE. Predictors were log-transformed in Results.

contribution.text: The N interval crosses zero and the d interval does not. This plot does not display the joint model, whose N coefficient is significant. Coefficients for different predictors should not be read as comparable standardized effect sizes.

sections.title: Survey study: researchers’ judgments
sections.role: Supplies separate evidence that the proposed heuristic is endorsed.

points.text: 215 scientists rated nine criteria; N M=3.84 versus effect size M=3.61, paired t(214)=3.21, p=.002. This is a rating comparison, not a replication outcome.

sections.title: Discussion: scope and alternatives
sections.role: Limits policy interpretation and returns to comprehensive study assessment.

points.text: Studies selected for replication and survey respondents are not representative; publication bias may contribute to the observed N–d relationship. Supporting files were listed but not read here.
The authors do not know causal policy effects and explicitly retain the importance of large samples; any rigid heuristic should be avoided.

sections.title: Supporting information and back matter
sections.role: Points to further materials without treating their listing as access.

points.text: The main-paper findings are readable, but robustness analyses in linked supplements and OSF data need independent retrieval before detailed verification.

explanation.text: Judging likely replication primarily by sample size; a diagnostic shortcut tested here, not a randomized policy.
A standardized mean difference; the paper harmonizes original effects into this unit.
Main outcome is a binary project-provided success indicator; its operationalization varies across replication projects.

An associated predictor can hide another predictor’s conditional relationship; here N becomes significant when effect size is included. This statistical description does not identify a causal mechanism.
Uncertainty interval for a coefficient; not the fraction of studies that replicated.
